# Model Architecture Modifications

Also called: NeRF Architecture Variants, NeRF Structural Changes

## Overview
Model Architecture Modifications encompass structural changes to the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework, which typically consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) mapping positional and directional encodings to volume density and color [S6]. These modifications address limitations in standard NeRF regarding geometric accuracy, rendering speed, handling of dynamic scenes, sparse inputs, and complex physical phenomena. Unlike sibling methods that focus on training hyperparameters or optimization loops, this family alters the network topology, input/output channels, or the underlying spatial representation (e.g., replacing MLPs with grids or SDFs) to enable new capabilities such as depth-of-field simulation, real-time rendering, or semantic understanding.

## Shared principles
The standard NeRF architecture [S6] serves as the baseline for these modifications. It consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a coarse network and a fine network. The coarse network takes positional encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ and outputs a latent feature vector $\mathbf{h}$ and volume density $\sigma$. The fine network takes $\mathbf{h}$, positional encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$, and positional encoded view direction $\gamma(\mathbf{d})$ to output color $\mathbf{c}$.

$$
\gamma(\mathbf{x}, d_1, d_2) = [\mathbf{x}, \sin(2^{d_1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{d_1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{d_2-1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{d_2-1}\pi\mathbf{x})]
$$

Modifications generally fall into three categories:
1.  **Input Expansion:** Adding new conditioning vectors (e.g., appearance embeddings $\mathbf{z}_i$, fluid volume $v$, or previous stage RGB) to the input concatenation.
2.  **Output Expansion:** Adding auxiliary heads to predict values other than $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{c}$, such as semantic labels $y_{aux}$, object codes $o$, or area encoding probabilities $p$. These are rendered using the same transmittance weights $T_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ as color:
    $$
    \hat{Y}(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T_i \alpha_i y_{aux}(x_i)
    $$
3.  **Representation Substitution:** Replacing the continuous MLP function with discrete structures (voxel grids, hash tables) or different implicit surfaces (SDFs).

## Subtopics

### [DoF-NeRF](9432-dof-nerf.md)
DoF-NeRF extends the standard NeRF architecture to simulate depth-of-field effects by introducing learnable aperture $K$ and focus distance $F$ parameters per view. It differs from standard NeRF by modeling the Circle of Confusion (CoC) diameter to blur out-of-focus regions, enabling the synthesis of all-in-focus views from shallow DoF inputs. Choose this when the input data exhibits lens blur and the goal is to recover a sharp 3D representation.

### [NeRF-VPT](11770-nerf-vpt.md)
NeRF-VPT uses a cascading view prompt tuning paradigm where the RGB output of a previous stage serves as a visual prompt for the next. It differs from standard NeRF by iteratively refining the network's output using internal RGB priors, improving quality in sparse-view settings without external networks. Choose this when standard NeRF fails to capture fine details due to limited input views.

### [MixRT](12401-mixrt.md)
MixRT is a hybrid representation combining a low-quality triangle mesh, a view-dependent displacement map, and a compressed NeRF model (Instant-NGP format). It differs from pure MLP-based NeRFs by offloading ray intersection to rasterizers and surface refinement to texture mapping units, enabling real-time rendering on edge devices. Choose this when real-time performance on constrained hardware is required.

### [Activation Feature Density Approximation](12492-activation-feature-density-approximation.md)
This method estimates volumetric density directly from intermediate activation features of the coarse MLP, replacing expensive fine network evaluations. It differs from SDF-based methods by retaining the standard density-based rendering formulation while optimizing the density prediction step itself. Choose this when inference speed is critical and the coarse network's activations correlate well with density.

### [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md)
SDF Representations replace volumetric density with a continuous scalar field representing the distance to the nearest surface. This approach addresses geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by defining geometry via a zero-level set. Choose this when explicit, sharp surface reconstruction is required.

### [Volume-Augmented NeRF](12973-volume-augmented-nerf.md)
Volume-Augmented NeRF binds an explicit fluid volume value $v_i$ to each sample point, allowing density and color to change over time due to fluid flow. It differs from static NeRF by integrating a differentiable fluid simulator's output into the radiance field. Choose this for dynamic scenes involving fluid dynamics.

### [Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture](12975-neural-pil-decomposition-architecture.md)
This architecture separates scene geometry, material properties, and illumination into distinct networks, predicting density, a BRDF embedding, and an illumination embedding. It differs from standard NeRF by decoupling appearance from geometry, enabling rendering under varying lighting conditions. Choose this when input images have inconsistent illumination.

### [Feature Fields](12995-feature-fields.md)
Feature Fields generalize NeRF by predicting arbitrary per-point feature signals $\mathbf{f}$ in addition to color and density. This allows encoding semantic labels, object codes, or latent embeddings directly into the volume rendering pipeline. Choose this when 3D-aware semantic understanding or object segmentation is needed.

### [SAID-NeRF](13619-said-nerf.md)
SAID-NeRF exploits instance masks from Visual Foundation Models to enhance surface estimation for transparent objects. It differs from standard NeRF by decomposing appearance into diffuse and specular components and using semantic segmentation to enforce higher surface densities. Choose this for reconstructing transparent objects with RGB-D data.

### [MINE](13661-mine.md)
MINE models the frustum of the source camera using a continuous depth Multiplane Image (MPI) representation, conditioned on input images. It differs from ray-based methods by reconstructing the frustum per plane, allowing rendering of any target view via homography warping after a single encoder pass. Choose this for efficient multi-view synthesis from a single source image.

### [Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations](13738-voxel-and-sparse-grid-representations.md)
These representations replace the continuous MLP with discrete structures like 3D voxel grids, hash tables, or triplanes. This substitution enables real-time differentiable volume rendering by computing color and density via interpolation. Choose this when training speed and inference latency are primary concerns.

### [Aleth-NeRF](13764-aleth-nerf.md)
Aleth-NeRF trains on under- and over-exposed images to render normal-light novel views by introducing 'Concealing Fields' that model light attenuation. It differs from RAW-NeRF by operating on standard 8-bit LDR images without pre-processing. Choose this for low-light or high-dynamic-range scene reconstruction from LDR inputs.

### [Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA)](13784-unified-volumetric-avatar-uva.md)
UVA represents dynamic human avatars by anchoring structured latent codes to a deformable mesh in canonical space. It distinguishes itself from UV mapping methods by enabling local and independent editing of geometry and texture. Choose this for animatable human avatars with local editing capabilities.

### [Gear-NeRF](13848-gear-nerf.md)
Gear-NeRF leverages semantic information to stratify dynamic scenes into motion-based 'gears', assigning higher resolution to regions with larger motion. It differs from uniform 4D sampling by using a series of 4D feature volumes, one per gear level. Choose this for efficient rendering of dynamic scenes with varying motion scales.

### [Transformer and Vision Model Integration](13911-transformer-and-vision-model-integration.md)
This family integrates Vision Transformers (ViT) into NeRF to leverage global semantic understanding and long-range dependencies. It solves the limitations of MLP-based NeRFs by either generalizing across scenes without per-scene tuning or explicitly modeling self-occlusion via attention. Choose this for single-image NeRF training or scenes with heavy occlusions.

### [Human and Specific Subject Modeling](13997-human-and-specific-subject-modeling.md)
This family focuses on architectures tailored for human avatars or specific subjects, often incorporating skeletal constraints or deformable meshes. It differs from general scene NeRFs by explicitly modeling articulation and pose-dependent appearance. Choose this for novel view synthesis of humans or articulated objects.

### [OPONeRF](14014-oponerf.md)
OPONeRF personalizes the parameters of the plenoptic mapping function for each sampled 3D point by dynamically conditioning network weights on the point's representation. It differs from vanilla NeRF by subdividing the scene and discriminatively responding to local variations. Choose this for handling test-time scene changes or perturbations.

### [Mixer-NeRF](14073-mixer-nerf.md)
Mixer-NeRF addresses the loss of local information in standard NeRF by introducing a hybrid spatial feature learning module (MLCA) and a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) network module. It sets itself apart by explicitly mixing spatial and channel features via fully connected layers before the main MLP inference. Choose this when standard NeRF produces blurry details.

### [SCALAR-NeRF](14267-scalar-nerf.md)
SCALAR-NeRF is a coarse-to-fine framework for scalable large-scale neural scene reconstruction that decomposes scenes into spatial blocks. It differs from Block-NeRF by fusing local outputs using a reference image rendered from the coarse global model, avoiding "foggy" artifacts. Choose this for training large-scale scenes on a single GPU.

### [Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization](14428-sparse-view-and-few-shot-optimization.md)
This family addresses overfitting and geometry breakdown in NeRF with drastically reduced input viewpoints. It mitigates ambiguity through in-situ regularization, deformable sampling, or pseudo-observation densification. Choose this when training data is extremely sparse ($|S| < 20$).

### [Mixture-of-Experts and Modular Architectures](14429-mixture-of-experts-and-modular-architectures.md)
This family replaces the single continuous function of NeRF with multiple specialized networks (experts) or parallel processing streams. It solves the limitations of conventional INRs by partitioning the input domain among distinct neural modules. Choose this for improving compression, training speed, or representation capacity in complex scenes.

### [Uncertainty and Reliability](14487-uncertainty-and-reliability.md)
Uncertainty methods extend NeRF architectures to quantify prediction confidence, modeling the scene as a probabilistic entity. Unlike deterministic variants, these methods provide pixel-level reliability metrics for color and depth. Choose this for robust filtering and conformal prediction in sparse or unstructured data.

### [Object Decomposition and Composition](14518-object-decomposition-and-composition.md)
This family explicitly separates a scene into distinct semantic or geometric object instances, enabling instance-level editing. It differs from Feature Fields by focusing on structural decomposition for editing rather than just semantic labeling. Choose this for amodal segmentation and object manipulation.

### [Lighting and Appearance Models](14522-lighting-and-appearance-models.md)
Lighting and Appearance Models modify the color prediction head to decouple scene geometry from illumination variations. They solve the problem of rendering failure in real-world collections with lighting changes by learning implicit appearance embeddings or explicit pre-integrated lighting. Choose this for "in-the-wild" photo collections.

### [Optimization and Training Procedures](14565-optimization-and-training-procedures.md)
This family covers algorithmic procedures for optimizing NeRF, often employing structural modifications to the optimization scope, such as skipping expensive fine-pass evaluations for empty rays. It differs from architecture changes by focusing on the training loop efficiency and convergence. Choose this for accelerating training or improving stability.

### [Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods](14566-image-enhancement-and-restoration-methods.md)
These methods address input degradation (blur, occlusions, low resolution) by integrating restoration mechanisms into the NeRF loop. They differ from standard NeRF by modeling the degradation process or separating static geometry from transient artifacts. Choose this when input images are not sharp or clean.

### [Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures](14567-modular-hierarchical-and-latent-architectures.md)
This family extends NeRF to handle non-rigid deformation with topological changes (HyperNeRF) or hierarchical scene structures (Strata-NeRF). It differs from standard NeRF by lifting canonical space to higher dimensions or using discrete latent codes to prevent cloudy artifacts. Choose this for dynamic non-rigid scenes or stratified environments.

### [NeRF-W](14630-nerf-w.md)
NeRF-W extends NeRF to handle unconstrained, "in-the-wild" photo collections by disentangling shared static geometry from image-dependent transient elements and photometric variations. It differs from NeRF-A and NeRF-U by combining appearance and uncertainty modeling. Choose this for reconstructing scenes with pedestrians and lighting changes.

### [Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF](14760-generalizable-implicit-reconstruction-with-srdf.md)
VolRecon uses a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) and a ray transformer to aggregate features from multi-view images. It differs from SDF-based methods by capturing both local geometric cues and global context, addressing over-smoothing. Choose this for generalizable implicit reconstruction with fine details.

### [MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields)](15007-murf-multi-baseline-radiance-fields.md)
MuRF is a feed-forward method for sparse view synthesis that constructs a target view frustum volume aligned with the target camera. It differs from reference-volume methods by using a 3D context-aware convolutional decoder, effectively aggregating multi-view information even with small overlap. Choose this for novel view synthesis under varying camera baselines.

### [Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations](15011-gaussian-and-primitive-based-representations.md)
This family replaces the continuous MLP with discrete geometric primitives or explicit Gaussian distributions. It differs from Voxel representations by using analytic primitives rather than voxel grids, and from SDFs by relying on alpha-blended primitives. Choose this for improved rendering efficiency and geometric fidelity.

### [Decentralized Federated NeRF](15032-decentralized-federated-nerf.md)
DecentNeRF learns global 3D scene representations from crowd-sourced images by distributing training to users and aggregating only global models. It differs from centralized approaches by preventing personal data leakage and handling transient personal content. Choose this for privacy-preserving large-scale scene reconstruction.

### [Tile and Slide Framework](15219-tile-and-slide-framework.md)
The Tile and Slide Framework (Snake-NeRF) scales NeRFs to large-scale Earth observation scenes by dividing the region into non-overlapping 3D tiles, each trained with its own NeRF. It differs from multi-GPU approaches by enforcing a strict single-device memory budget. Choose this for out-of-core training of massive scenes.

### [Neural Proxy](15220-neural-proxy.md)
Neural Proxy represents photo-realistic targets as animatable proxies, combining neural volume rendering with neural texture. It differs from NeRF by tying content to an animatable mesh proxy, allowing unseen animations. Choose this for synthesizing unseen animations of photo-realistic targets.

### NeRF-VAE
- **Definition:** A generative NeRF model that generalizes to out-of-distribution scenes and removes the need to train on each scene from scratch [S1].
- **Steps:** The NeRF renderer is conditioned on a latent code trained using Iterative Amortized Inference and a ResNet encoder. An attention-based scene function is introduced instead of the typical MLP [S1].
- **Comparison:** Outperforms baseline NeRF with a low number of scene views (5-20), but is outperformed by baseline NeRF when a large number of views are available (100+) due to lower scene expressivity [S1].

### PIE-NeRF
- **Definition:** A pipeline integrating physics-based elastodynamic simulation with a neural radiance field representation, using a meshless discretisation based on quadratic generalized moving least squares on top of the density field of a NeRF [S1].
- **Steps:** Enables large deformations and nonlinear hyperelastic material simulation directly on the implicit representation and supports interactive manipulation of real-world captured scenes with complex geometries [S1].

### DäRF Implementation Details
- **Parameters:** NeRF Backbone: K-planes [36]. MDE Model: DPT-hybrid [38]. Optimizer: Adam [21]. NeRF Learning Rate: 1e-2. MDE Learning Rate: 1e-5. LR Schedule: Cosine warmup [S2, unofficial].

### NeRF Model Architecture
- **Definition:** The neural network architecture for NeRF, consisting of dense layers with ReLU activations, potentially using view directions as input [S3, unofficial].
- **Parameters:** `D`: The depth of the network (number of hidden layers). Default is 8. `input_ch_views`: The number of input channels for view directions. Default is 3. `output_ch`: The number of output channels. Default is 4 (RGB + density). `use_viewdirs`: Boolean flag to determine if view directions are used as input to the network [S3, unofficial].

### S3-NeRF
- **Definition:** A method using shadow and shading cues to infer scene geometry and enable single-image NeRF training [S1].
- **Steps:** Employ a UNISURF-based occupancy field 3D representation instead of density. Use a modified physics-based rendering equation. Use occupancy-based shadow calculation [S1].

### KiloNeRF-style Grid Distillation
- **Definition:** Distills a large teacher NeRF into a spatially partitioned grid of tiny MLPs to enable fast, adaptive evaluation by mapping 3D positions to local student networks [S4, unofficial].
- **Steps:** Initialize a dictionary mapping 3D grid cell indices (i,j,k) to TinyMLP instances. For each training iteration, sample a random ray and generate num_samples stratified samples along it. Compute the grid cell index for each sample by normalizing its position within the bounding box and scaling by grid resolution. Accumulate L2 loss between student and teacher outputs across all samples. Update all grid MLPs using the accumulated loss and the configured learning rate [S4, unofficial].
- **Parameters:** grid_resolution: 3D tuple defining the number of cells per axis, e.g., (16,16,16). num_distill_iterations: Number of distillation optimization steps, e.g., 1000. num_samples: Number of stratified samples per ray, e.g., 384. learning_rate: Optimization step size for grid MLP updates, e.g., 1e-3. bmin, bmax: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the scene bounds, e.g., [0,0,0] and [1,1,1] [S4, unofficial].

### NeRF with Time Parameter
- **Steps:** Add a time parameter to the model inputs to adapt NeRF for dynamic scenes. Positionally encode the time parameter and concatenate it with the positional encoding of spatial coordinates $\gamma_x(\mathbf{x})$ [S5].
- **Parameters:** Train using the configuration reported for NeRF's real forward-facing experiments [S5].
- **Comparison:** Adding a time parameter improves quality over vanilla NeRF but still lacks detail, suffers from blurry predictions, and fails to reason about scene dynamics [S5].

### StylizedNeRF
- **Steps:** Utilizes a mutual learning strategy to optimize both the stylized NeRF and the 2D stylization network. Handles ambiguities of the 2D stylized results via learnable latent codes, ensuring consistency in geometry [S6].

### NeRF-Editing
- **Definition:** The first mesh-based shape deformation method, leveraging explicit representations for scene geometry edits and implicit representations for realistic rendering effects [S6].
- **Steps:** 1. Extract explicit triangular mesh from NeRF. 2. Enable intuitive user-driven deformations through classic ARAP deformation method. 3. Generate tetrahedral mesh around triangular mesh to propagate deformations spatially. 4. Employ tetrahedral vertex interpolation to transform discrete deformations into continuous field. 5. Ensure rays passing through mesh bend according to user adjustments [S6].

### NeuralEditor
- **Definition:** A method employing a point cloud-guided NeRF model for shape manipulation, leveraging K-D trees and deterministic integration strategy for accurate point cloud-based rendering, with Phong reflection modeling to enhance color fidelity and geometric detail [S6].
- **Steps:** 1. Employ point cloud-guided NeRF model. 2. Leverage K-D trees. 3. Use deterministic integration strategy. 4. Achieve accurate point cloud-based rendering. 5. Apply Phong reflection modeling [S6].

### Shared G-MLP
- **Definition:** A shared geometry MLP that enables the constraint of multi-view consistency to be propagated from the NeRF branch to the detection branch [S7].
- **Number:** Without the shared G-MLP, performance drops from 50.1 to 48.1 mAP@.25, as the influence of multi-view consistency is only propagated into the image backbone [S7].

### Mip-NeRF
- **Definition:** A method that approximates cone tracing instead of using the ray tracing of standard NeRF volume rendering to achieve inherent multi-scale representation and automatic anti-aliasing, outperforming baseline NeRF especially at lower resolutions [S1].
- **Steps:** To generate an individual pixel, a cone is cast from the camera center along the viewing direction through the center of the pixel. The cone is approximated by a multivariate Gaussian whose mean vector and covariance matrix are derived to match the appropriate geometry [S1].
- **Formula:** The Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) is calculated as: $\gamma(\mu, \Sigma) = E_{x \sim N(\mu, \Sigma)}[\gamma(x)] = \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\mu_\gamma) \odot \exp(-(1/2)\text{diag}(\Sigma_\gamma)) \\ \cos(\mu_\gamma) \odot \exp(-(1/2)\text{diag}(\Sigma_\gamma)) \end{bmatrix}$, where $\mu_\gamma, \Sigma_\gamma$ are the means and variances of the multivariate Gaussian lifted onto the positional encoding basis with N levels [S1].
- **Comparison:** Unlike standard NeRF which uses ray tracing, Mip-NeRF uses cone tracing via IPE, resulting in automatic anti-aliasing and better performance at lower resolutions [S1].

## Background
The standard NeRF architecture was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [S1][S3, unofficial]. Subsequent works have modified this architecture to address various limitations, including speed (KiloNeRF, Instant-NGP), geometric accuracy (SDF-based methods), dynamic scenes (NeRF with Time Parameter, Volume-Augmented NeRF), and sparse inputs (MINE, MuRF). The family has grown to include specialized variants for specific domains such as human avatars (UVA), transparent objects (SAID-NeRF), and large-scale scenes (SCALAR-NeRF, Tile and Slide Framework).
